content:
TL;DR
Five layers: React/MUI, Flask APIs, analytics, edge execution, and SQLite persistence. A bounded deque batches recent samples (500 records or ~5s) but is not a durable queue. PHM uses RMS/FFT, One-Class SVM, DTW, and PCA drift monitoring; engineers interpret results. AI agents are controlled clients: the backend enforces allowlists, authorization, validation, and audit logging. Deployment starts as a Docker Compose edge monolith; decouple workers only when measurements justify it. Bottom line: Reliability comes from traceable data, explicit failure behavior, and governed agents.
This article describes an Edge AI / Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) platform from a system-design perspective: architecture, data flow, analytical methods, backend, AI agents, deployment, failure handling, and trade-offs.
1. Project Overview The platform turns equipment signals into information engineers can use to investigate health and plan maintenance. The main workflow:
flowchart LR A[Sensor Data] --> B[Feature Engineering] B --> C[ML Analysis] C --> D[Edge Inference] D --> E[Health Monitoring] E --> F[AI Agent] F --> G[Engineering Decision]The platform provides four capabilities:
Capability Purpose Sensor-data processing Collect, organize, and transform equipment signals into usable data Feature engineering and ML Extract signal characteristics, identify unusual patterns, and support health assessment Health monitoring Track health scores, historical changes, and potential abnormal conditions AI-assisted workflows Retrieve relevant data, summarize findings, and help engineers investigate the next step The AI agent is an assistance layer, not an autonomous replacement for engineering judgment.
2. Why Edge AI? A model is only one part of a production system; the data path and operational controls decide whether it is useful.
2.1 Common engineering challenges Integration complexity. Data acquisition, preprocessing, model execution, APIs, dashboards, and alerts often live in different components; without clear interfaces, a small change can ripple across modules.
Data lineage. Engineers need to know which data, model, and configuration produced a feature or score; without traceability, analyses are hard to reproduce or compare.
Deployment latency. A solution that works in development can still be hard to package, configure, install, and update at a site.
2.2 The intended improvement The platform standardizes the path from ingestion to operational use.
Engineering area Intended outcome Deployment Reduce the effort required to package and release a platform update Integration Reuse common interfaces instead of repeatedly writing project-specific integration code Data lineage Make analysis inputs, outputs, and model versions easier to trace Maintenance workflow Present data and analysis in a form that supports investigation and follow-up The source slides show three metrics — deployment cycle, integration code, and lineage synchronization — to be read with their definitions and baselines; they do not prove model accuracy or data quality.
3. System Architecture flowchart TB subgraph UI["L1 User & Frontend"] A["React + MUI"] B["Workflow UI / React Flow"] end subgraph API["L2 Backend Core"] C["Flask REST APIs"] D["Authentication and Job Coordination"] end subgraph ML["L3 ML & Analytics"] E["Feature Engineering"] F["ML / PHM Algorithms"] G["Health Score and Drift Analysis"] end subgraph EDGE["L4 Edge Execution"] H["Sensor / File Inputs"] I["Edge Runtime and Inference"] end subgraph DATA["L5 Data & Persistence"] J["edge_ai.db"] K["vibration.db"] L["Model and Analysis Artifacts"] end A --> C B --> C C --> D D --> E E --> F F --> G H --> I I --> E D --> J E --> K F --> L3.1 Five layers Layer Responsibility L1 Frontend React UI, dashboard, and agent UI L2 Backend Flask APIs, authentication, and tool coordination L3 Analytics Feature engineering, model training, and anomaly detection L4 Edge Sensor access, edge runtime, and inference L5 Data SQLite, model files, and history Layering is a responsibility boundary, not independent microservices: the frontend does not access the database directly, and inference is separate from UI so it can be reused.
Edge execution runs locally to keep high-frequency samples off the central service; the split depends on latency, compute, network, data volume, and deployment.
3.2 Frontend and backend collaboration The frontend uses React 18, Material UI, and React Flow; the backend uses Flask REST APIs with Blueprints for sensors, models, devices, users, and agents.
REST API: query data, update settings, submit training jobs. Polling: fetch equipment status periodically. SSE: receive server events and agent streams. 3.3 Performance metrics Latency metrics need consistent start and end points, must distinguish average, P95, P99, and cold start, and should not be summed across sources.
4. End-to-End Data Flow The data flow defines how data enters, is processed, and stays stable under bursts.
flowchart LR A["Sensor /<br/>File Input"] --> B["In-Memory<br/>Buffer"] B --> C{"Batch<br/>Trigger<br/>(time or size)"}flowchart LR D["Persist /<br/>Prepare Batch"] --> E["Feature<br/>Extraction"] E --> F["ML / PHM<br/>Analysis"]flowchart LR G["Health Score<br/>and Anomaly<br/>Results"] --> H["Dashboard /<br/>Report / Alert"] H --> I["Engineer<br/>Review and<br/>Action"]4.1 Buffering and batching Sensors produce data continuously; a bounded deque(maxlen=5000) buffers samples and flushes up to 500 records to SQLite every ~5s or when the batch threshold is reached, keeping high-frequency I/O from competing with queries.
At capacity it discards the oldest samples: a useful memory bound, not a durable queue. If every sample must survive, add a persistent queue, overflow handling, backpressure, and loss monitoring.
flowchart LR A["Sensor Stream"] --> B["Bounded In-Memory Queue"] B --> C["Batch Flush Worker"] C --> D["SQLite Persistence"]4.2 Feature extraction and analysis The batch yields features, anomaly indicators, a health score, and metadata.
4.3 Results and action The platform presents results through dashboards, reports, or alerts; anomaly detection identifies deviation, while root-cause analysis explains it and needs history, equipment knowledge, and engineer validation—not a score alone.
5. Machine Learning and PHM Methods PHM systems combine domain knowledge, signal processing, statistical analysis, and machine learning. No single algorithm answers every equipment-health question.
5.1 Signal features Common signal features include:
RMS (root mean square): summarizes magnitude; often used for vibration energy. Peak: captures the largest absolute amplitude in a window. Kurtosis: measures tail behavior and can flag impulsive signals. Interpretation depends on the distribution and implementation. FFT (Fast Fourier Transform): converts a time-domain signal into frequency components, revealing dominant frequencies and spectral changes. For a signal \(x = [x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N]\), RMS is defined as:
$$ \mathrm{RMS} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2} $$Feature definitions, window sizes, sampling rates, units, and preprocessing should be consistent. Otherwise, apparent changes may come from the pipeline rather than the equipment.
5.2 One-Class SVM for anomaly detection One-Class Support Vector Machine (One-Class SVM) learns the boundary of normal data and flags observations outside it. It suits cases with few labeled faults.
Important considerations include:
Fit on a representative baseline of normal operation. Scale features consistently. Tune nu and gamma with validation data and feedback. Monitor false positives and negatives; an anomaly score is not a diagnosis. Revisit the baseline when conditions or equipment change. flowchart LR A["Historical Normal Data"] --> B["Feature Scaling"] B --> C["Train One-Class SVM"] C --> D["Learn Decision Boundary"] D --> E["New Feature Vector: Normal or Anomaly"]5.3 Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) Dynamic Time Warping measures similarity between sequences that differ in timing or duration. It helps compare patterns whose events are shifted in time.
DTW uses a cumulative-cost matrix with recurrence:
$$ D(i,j) = d(x_i,y_j) + \min\left\{ D(i-1,j),\; D(i,j-1),\; D(i-1,j-1) \right\} $$where \(d(x_i,y_j)\) is the local distance. A warping window cuts computation and prevents implausible alignments. DTW is not universal; results depend on references, distance metric, normalization, and domain.
5.4 PCA for data-drift monitoring Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projects correlated features into fewer dimensions. Comparing current data with a baseline reveals distribution changes.
Drift does not mean failure; a changed recipe, sensor replacement, operating regime, or preprocessing change can all produce it.
flowchart LR A["Historical Baseline Features"] --> B["Fit PCA Model"] B --> C["Reference Feature Space"] C --> D["New Features: Projection and Drift Analysis"]5.5 Choosing the method Method Primary purpose Key limitation RMS / Peak / Kurtosis Summarize time-domain signal characteristics Can be sensitive to windowing, noise, and operating conditions FFT Identify spectral components and frequency changes Requires appropriate sampling and interpretation One-Class SVM Detect deviations from a learned normal-data boundary Depends on baseline quality and parameter selection DTW Compare sequences with temporal misalignment Can be computationally expensive and reference-dependent PCA Monitor multivariate structure and potential drift Drift is not equivalent to failure The methods are complementary; validate combinations against the equipment and data.
6. Backend Design 6.1 Flask application structure Flask Blueprints separate API areas by responsibility: sensor data, ML analysis, edge management, maintenance, agent, and user/admin. Blueprints organize routes; they do not fix coupling. When business logic concentrates in one module, extract a service layer and data-access layer.
6.2 Authentication and authorization LDAP / AD verifies identity; JWTs authenticate later API calls. Authorization is checked per protected operation. Tokens need expiry and signing; secrets must never be hard-coded. A valid token still requires role and resource checks; hiding a button is not authorization.
flowchart LR A["User Login"] --> B["LDAP / AD Authentication"] B --> C["Issue JWT Access Token"] C --> D["Authorized API Requests"] D --> E["Backend Permission Checks"]6.3 SQLite and data separation edge_ai.db — application records, configuration, model history. vibration.db — vibration data and alerts. SQLAlchemy manages access; ATTACH DATABASE supports cross-database queries. Separate files do not provide cross-database atomicity; transactions, backups, migrations, and concurrent writes still need testing.
6.4 Scheduled tasks and model history APScheduler runs periodic jobs such as drift checks, reports, or maintenance summaries. Jobs must tolerate retries, failures, and partial completion. Starting the scheduler in multiple web workers can duplicate jobs; use a dedicated scheduler or single-owner mechanism. Model-build history records model version, training-data reference, configuration, timestamp, and evaluation results. Builds need explicit states so a failed run differs from one that never started:
stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> building building --> completed building --> failed7. AI Agent: From Data Retrieval to Assisted Investigation An AI agent translates a natural-language request into a controlled sequence of data retrieval and analysis. The constraints are permissions, traceability, and execution boundaries.
7.1 Example tools The agent may expose:
Tool Responsibility get_health_score Health score and context get_vibration_data Authorized vibration data run_sql_query_safe Constrained read-only query anomaly_detection Defined anomaly workflow read_file Allowlisted files export_report Report from validated inputs Tool names are illustrative; only implemented tools are available.
7.2 Agent flow flowchart TD A["User Request"] --> B["LLM Planner / Orchestrator"] B --> C["Select an Approved Tool"] C --> D["Backend Validation and Authorization"] D --> E["Execute Tool"] E --> F["Structured Result"] F --> G{"More Evidence Needed?"} G -->|"Yes"| B G -->|"No"| H["LLM Summary"] H --> I["Response / Report for Human Review"]The LLM plans and selects tools; the backend executes SQL, file access, and computation. This reduces fabricated live values but does not eliminate hallucination; answers should cite query results, time ranges, and data sources.
7.3 Tool governance and safety The model proposes actions; the backend enforces the rules:
Validate arguments against a schema; require confirmation for consequential actions. Authenticate the user and authorize the requested asset and data. Use allowlists for files, tools, and queryable resources. Restrict database operations; no arbitrary destructive SQL. Apply timeouts, output-size limits, and audit logging; return structured errors without exposing secrets. A prompt instruction is not a security boundary; enforcement belongs in the application and tools.
7.4 Planning vs execution The LLM understands the request, plans, and summarizes; Python tools execute queries and computation; the backend enforces permissions, validation, and execution boundaries. This makes computation testable but adds orchestration, latency, and failure points; compare it with a single-model or deterministic workflow.
7.5 Server-Sent Events (SSE) SSE streams progress and partial results over HTTP, so users see multi-step work as it happens. Define event types, error behavior, timeouts, and reconnection. Streaming does not replace backend logging or durable job state; evaluate WebSocket only if bidirectional interaction is needed.
8. Deployment and Observability 8.1 Docker Compose Docker Compose manages frontend, backend, and persistent volumes, standardizing dependencies, ports, environment variables, and startup order. A healthy container does not mean the application works; readiness checks should verify critical dependencies, and data belongs in volumes.
8.2 Runtime frontend configuration When the frontend is a static bundle and the backend URL varies by environment, a runtime env.js can expose the endpoint through window.ENV, avoiding a rebuild per environment. Load it before application code, validate it at startup, and treat it as public. Never put secrets in browser-visible variables.
flowchart LR A["Docker Image"] --> B["Container Entrypoint"] B --> C["Runtime Environment Variables"] C --> D["env.js"] D --> E["window.ENV"] E --> F["Frontend API Endpoint"]8.3 Monitoring API request rate, latency, and error rate. Ingestion delay, queue depth, batch size, and dropped samples. Model execution duration and analysis failures. Scheduler job start time, duration, and outcome. Agent tool-call success rate, timeouts, and cost. Disk usage, database growth, and artifact storage. Observability should answer three questions: what failed, where, and whether the system can recover safely.
9. Failure Handling and Scaling Failure handling must be designed into the data path, not added after an incident.
Failure Risk Mitigation Buffer full Old samples may be dropped Track drops; use durable buffering if loss is unacceptable Source unavailable Stale or incomplete analysis Track freshness; surface missing data; do not treat stale values as current Model fails Missing or invalid result Record context, bounded retries, keep the last valid result with a timestamp SQLite contention Delayed or failed writes Reduce competing writers, batch writes, tune transactions, or migrate Duplicate scheduled task Duplicate reports or work Single scheduler owner, idempotent jobs, or coordination LLM or tool timeout Incomplete agent workflow Timeouts, bounded retries, structured errors, visible partial state Network interrupted Remote service unavailable Keep local capabilities, queue recoverable work, define synchronization 9.1 Evolve in stages Scaling should respond to measured constraints, not technology fashion.
flowchart LR A["Stage 1: Edge Monolith"] --> B["Stage 2: Decoupled Pipeline"] B --> C["Stage 3: Cloud / Multi-Node Scale-Out"]Stage 1 — Edge monolith. A compact Flask app, local persistence, and local inference suit a single node with modest load.
Stage 2 — Decoupled pipeline. When ingestion and analysis hurt API responsiveness, add durable queues and separate workers; retries and backpressure become easier.
Stage 3 — Cloud or multi-node scale-out. When workload, availability, or concurrency demands it, consider a server database, shared job coordination, centralized observability, and horizontal scaling; keep latency-sensitive work at the edge.
MQTT, durable brokers, Redis, PostgreSQL, and load balancers are future options, not current components.
flowchart LR A["Sensors / Edge Devices"] --> B["MQTT Broker"] B --> C["Durable Message Queue"] C --> D["Worker Cluster"] D --> E["ML Inference"] D --> F["PostgreSQL"] D --> G["Redis Cache"] E --> H["Flask API"] F --> H G --> H H --> I["Frontend"]10. Engineering Trade-offs The goal is not the most sophisticated technology in every layer, but a reliable current system with a practical path forward.
Area Current approach Benefit Trade-off / next consideration Web backend Flask Lightweight and straightforward to organize Long-running tasks may need separate workers Persistence / scheduling / buffering SQLite, APScheduler, bounded deque Simple local operation Concurrency, duplicate jobs, and non-durable buffering need explicit handling Frontend updates REST APIs and SSE Familiar request-response model with optional streaming Reconnection and job state must be designed ML / PHM Feature engineering plus multiple analytical methods Combines interpretable signal features with statistical and ML methods Requires baseline validation and domain-specific interpretation Deployment Docker Compose Repeatable single-host deployment Not a complete orchestration solution for large clusters Separate what exists today from what may come later; this keeps a roadmap from being mistaken for a production capability.
11. Conclusion Design the complete data path and make results traceable. A model is only useful when its inputs, outputs, errors, and context are handled reliably, with versioning and lineage for comparison. Treat AI agents as controlled application clients. The backend, not the prompt, enforces permissions, validation, and tool safety. Make failure behavior explicit. Buffers, schedulers, databases, network dependencies, and model calls all need defined failure semantics. Scale based on evidence. Start with deployment constraints, then decouple or replace components when measurements justify it. The value is not the number of frameworks, but the engineering judgment to make them work together safely and predictably.
Terms of use: For technical exchange only. Company, customer, and internal-project identifiers are removed; data and scenarios are de-identified or virtualized. Future architectures are possible directions, not deployment claims. Licensing follows the author’s published terms.

title: Designing a Semiconductor Equipment Edge AI Platform: From Sensor Data to Intelligent Decisions

content:
TL;DR
Six-layer architecture: sensing → streaming → signal processing → PHM → Edge Agent → MES/EAP safety integration. Two-stage detection (Isolation Forest → Autoencoder) plus RUL prediction turns raw signals into maintenance planning; figures are project-specific. Models ship through shadow deployment, canary rollout (5% → 20% → 100%), then monitoring and rollback. Edge Agent, Industrial RAG, and MLOps connect evidence to workflows, but safety-critical control stays outside the LLM. Make each layer observable, verifiable, and recoverable before expanding autonomy.
Introduction This article expands an 11-slide interview deck into a technical reference on the Smart Fab Edge AI architecture. The appendix explains how to read the figures.
It covers real-time processing, anomaly detection, Remaining Useful Life (RUL) prediction, edge deployment, industrial knowledge retrieval, and AI agent boundaries. The real question is not how to deploy models, but how to run them under constrained resources — balancing latency, compute, reliability, and operating cost — while integrating with existing controls, maintenance workflows, and factory systems.
Download Introduction — narrated by Morty Intellectual Property and Usage Notice: This article is for technical exchange, architecture discussion, and demonstration of personal capability. The content has been de-identified. It contains no confidential customer data, trade secrets, or non-public project information. Use and redistribution of the text and diagrams are subject to the author’s published licensing terms.
01. System Objectives and Design Assumptions Semiconductor lines have many equipment types, high-frequency sensor data, expensive downtime, and strict latency and reliability requirements for some control loops. The architecture therefore pairs edge computing with centralized management: latency-sensitive work stays in the factory, while centralized services handle management. Firewall and audit rules also make sending data off-site for real-time analysis impractical.
Data governance and security: Classify and control access to sensor data, equipment information, and maintenance records; process sensitive data in-factory and follow internal rules for cross-system transfers. Edge resources: Choose model size, inference frequency, and buffering against each device’s CPU, memory, and accelerators. Detection usability: Beyond accuracy, evaluate false-positive and false-negative rates, alert volume, and on-site workload. Safety and fault isolation: AI assesses anomalies and recommends maintenance; safety-critical control stays with validated control systems and safety mechanisms. 02. End-to-End Technical Architecture The architecture has six layers. The first three answer where data comes from, how it is organized, and how it becomes a judgment; the last three answer who receives that judgment, under what permissions, and how it connects to existing systems.
Layer Name Key Technologies and Responsibilities 01 Sensing and Data Acquisition MCUs, IO-Link, vibration/current/pressure sensors 02 Streaming and Time-Series Data Kafka, InfluxDB, ring buffers, timestamps, and synchronization 03 Signal Processing FFT, wavelet transforms, time-domain and frequency-domain feature extraction 04 AI Analytics and PHM Isolation Forest, Autoencoders, LSTM/Transformer, and RUL prediction 05 Edge Agent and Task Orchestration State management, tool routing, workflow orchestration, and model selection 06 Integration and Safety Control SECS/GEM, MES/EAP APIs, authorization, and safety middleware Edge devices handle low-latency processing and inference. The central platform manages models, runs cross-equipment analytics and training, and coordinates deployment.
These components need not form a linear pipeline; the right combination depends on data frequency, latency, and deployment environment.
Even if a model returns in milliseconds, end-to-end latency must include acquisition, signal processing, inference, communication, and controller execution.
03. High-Throughput Data Streaming and Signal Processing In high-frequency sensing, the first challenge is rarely model accuracy — it is processing a continuous stream of incoming data.
Data Volume and Scope Take 20 machines, three sensor channels each, sampled continuously at 2 kHz, with each sample stored as 4 bytes.
Per second:
$$ 20 \times 3 \times 2{,}000 \times 4 = 480{,}000\ \text{bytes/s} $$Per day:
$$ 480{,}000 \times 86{,}400 = 41{,}472{,}000{,}000\ \text{bytes/day} $$That is about 41.47 GB/day in decimal units (1 GB = \(10^9\) bytes). This counts raw values only — not timestamps, packet overhead, indexes, storage formats, or other metadata. With those, real traffic or storage can approach 50 GB/day.
The 20-machine figure is an illustrative calculation, not a scale claim. Managed fleet size (how many machines the system can connect to) and high-frequency processing scale (how many actually stream raw waveforms at 2 kHz) are different metrics. Managing 500+ machines does not mean all of them stream raw waveforms at that rate.
Signal Processing Pipeline Acquisition: Capture vibration, current, and pressure signals, handling timestamps, missing values, and data quality. Windowing: Split continuous signals into fixed-length windows; length and overlap follow equipment characteristics and analysis needs. Feature extraction: Apply FFT, wavelet transforms, and statistics to compute RMS, spectral entropy, and band energy. Output: Emit fixed-format feature vectors for anomaly detection and health models. A model might consume a 64-dimensional feature vector instead of the full waveform, cutting downstream compute. Suitability still depends on the anomaly pattern — information lost during extraction cannot be recovered later.
Edge Optimization Process in batches or windows instead of sample by sample. Use preallocated ring buffers to cut allocation and copying. Separate high-frequency signal processing from lower-frequency state analysis. Apply different retention and transmission policies to raw data, features, and events. Monitor queue length, data loss, CPU usage, and end-to-end latency. 04. Two-Stage Anomaly Detection Equipment failure datasets are heavily imbalanced: normal data is easy to collect, real failures are rare. Pure supervised learning therefore lacks enough labeled failures.
False alarms are the other practical problem. Most come from material changeover or warm-up, when the vibration spectrum briefly departs from its usual distribution. The model scores it as anomalous and fires repeatedly while the machine is fine — enough noise for on-site staff to start ignoring the system.
This architecture therefore separates cheap initial screening from deeper assessment.
Stage 1: Rapid Screening Isolation Forest flags samples that differ from observed data. It is lightweight enough for some resource-constrained edge environments. Its job is to shortlist data for investigation, not to declare failure.
Stage 2: In-Depth Assessment An Autoencoder measures reconstruction error against learned normal patterns. Thresholds can be set per equipment type, operating state, and sensor channel, so normal process transitions and load changes are not classified as failures.
Alert Consolidation Alert management cannot rely on model output alone. It must also consider repeated alerts from the same machine, alert duration and severity, the machine’s operating and maintenance state, and whether an alert is already acknowledged or tied to a work order. A five-minute duplicate-suppression window per equipment and anomaly type is a reasonable starting point, with exceptions preserved for severity escalation and safety events.
05. Equipment Health Management and Remaining Useful Life Prediction Anomaly detection answers “is the equipment deviating from normal?” Predictive maintenance goes further: “how is health changing?” and “when will maintenance be needed?”
Equipment health management (PHM) combines sensor features, equipment history, failure modes, and maintenance records. With enough data, an RUL model estimates time to a defined failure condition.
RUL Model Design Statistical / survival analysis: e.g. Weibull distributions, given appropriate assumptions. Time-series models: LSTM or Transformer, tracking how health indicators evolve. Domain features: band energy, spectral entropy, vibration amplitude, and load, to sharpen recognition of real failure modes. A Weibull distribution alone does not make a single machine’s RUL accurate; per-machine prediction still needs observations and validation.
From Prediction to Planning RUL matters because it lets maintenance teams plan people, spare parts, and downtime in advance.
Routine monitoring: RUL > 30 days — keep tracking at the established cadence. Advance preparation: 7–30 days — verify spare parts and maintenance resources. Priority assessment: < 7 days — schedule an engineering inspection and evaluate the maintenance window. These thresholds are illustrative. Real ones depend on failure consequences, spare-part lead times, prediction uncertainty, and production scheduling. For safety-critical equipment, continued operation must not rest on the RUL estimate alone.
Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) is an aggregate metric: it weights large misses more heavily and is not a per-prediction guarantee.
06. Edge Deployment and Model Lifecycle Management After training, the next problem is deploying reliably across devices and lines — and restoring the previous version when an update fails. In a factory this is more than packaging a container: OS, hardware architecture, drivers, inference-engine versions, and equipment protocols all affect whether the model runs.
1. Standardized Packaging Bundle the model, inference application, dependencies, and config into a versioned, traceable artifact. Run compatibility tests per hardware platform.
2. Shadow Deployment Run the new model alongside the current model or rules without affecting production control. Compare outputs, latency, resource use, and representative failure cases. Cover a representative range of operating conditions; two weeks is a reference, not a rule for equipment with rare failures.
3. Canary Release Deploy to a small subset, then expand — for example 5%, 20%, then 100%, with explicit acceptance criteria at each stage.
4. Monitoring and Rollback Track inference failure rate, latency, resource use, and output distribution. If a threshold is crossed, stop the rollout and revert to a validated version.
On top of this, a self-service interface lets production engineers with the right permissions select versions, inspect deployment status, and roll back without touching model internals.
07. Edge Agent: Task Orchestration and Decision Boundaries An Edge Agent turns sensor data, model inference, equipment states, and maintenance procedures into an executable, traceable workflow.
It does not need an LLM for every decision. For tasks with strict latency and well-defined inputs and outputs, conventional logic or lightweight models are easier to test and validate. Agents fit cross-tool coordination, information integration, and multi-step execution.
Task Allocation at the Edge Real-time signal processing: Acquisition, feature extraction, and necessary low-latency inference at the edge. State assessment and orchestration: Combine anomaly scores, RUL, equipment state, and maintenance records to decide whether further inspection or a work order is needed. Equipment control and safety: Executed by systems with explicit control logic and validated safety mechanisms. Free-form text or unvalidated model output must never become a high-risk control command. Workflow frameworks such as LangGraph manage agent state, tool calls, retries, and branches. A model router can pick a model or rule engine based on task complexity, latency, and available compute. Neither guarantees real-time behavior or safety — execution time, error handling, resource limits, and exceptional paths still need testing.
Handling Disconnections The network is down. Should the Agent keep working or stop?
Essential monitoring and local state assessment keep running on predefined rules when upstream is lost. If the system cannot confirm its own state, it enters a predefined degraded mode — and what each device does in that mode comes from equipment-specific risk analysis, not from a general-purpose Agent.
Keep three concepts distinct:
Offline availability: Can local monitoring or inference continue during an outage? Task success: Can the Agent complete tool calls, state updates, and work orders? Equipment safety: Do existing controllers still protect the equipment during failures? Task success cannot substitute for safety validation. For OHT and other high-risk equipment, safety must rest on independent mechanisms and verification.
08. Industrial RAG: Making Equipment Knowledge Searchable and Traceable Factory knowledge lives beyond equipment manuals — in maintenance logs, fault analysis reports, engineering notes, and historical work orders. Formats, naming, and quality are inconsistent. Dumping documents into a vector database can produce fluent answers that are neither correct nor applicable to the equipment’s current state.
Industrial RAG is therefore about traceability first: connecting questions, retrieved evidence, and source documents.
Knowledge Pipeline Document preparation and access control: Convert formats, remove duplicates, identify versions, handle sensitive data, and preserve provenance and permissions. Semantic chunking and indexing: Split documents by structure and content, then generate vector representations. Hybrid retrieval: Combine BM25, vector search, and metadata filtering to cope with terminology, equipment IDs, and near-duplicate documents. Reranking: Reassess candidate relevance to the question. Answer generation and citations: Generate from retrieved evidence and cite original documents, versions, and pages so users can verify. Enterprise Constraints Deploying RAG in a factory raises questions about document-level permissions in retrieval results, whether the model can reach unauthorized data, and how conflicting or outdated documents are handled.
Maintenance recommendations should clearly separate what the source documents state from what the model inferred. When evidence is insufficient, the system should say so rather than invent a complete-looking procedure.
Indexes and query logs need retention periods, auditing, and access permissions matched to data sensitivity.
09. MLOps: Continuous Monitoring After Model Deployment The model performs well on the test set. Then what?
Component wear, maintenance activity, load changes, or process changes can shift the data distribution away from training. Deployed models therefore need continuous monitoring and a workflow connecting detection, evaluation, and version updates.
Drift Monitoring Depending on the data, use PSI, the KS test, or other distribution-difference measures against a baseline. PSI above 0.25 is a common warning threshold, but exceeding it does not mean the model has failed; thresholds should follow data distributions, feature behavior, and validation results.
Monitor missing data, sensor anomalies, inference latency, and output distribution too, so sensor failures are not misread as model drift. A seven-day rolling baseline must not slowly absorb developing anomalies. More robust: dynamic baselines by operating mode, plus anomaly checks and explicit baseline-update conditions.
Model Update Workflow Periodically evaluate data quality and model performance. Build candidate models for confirmed issues. Validate against historical data and relevant simulated scenarios. Compare old and new in shadow mode. Release incrementally after required reviews. Preserve version, data provenance, parameters, and validation records for traceability and rollback. Automation is not about replacing a model the moment drift appears. It is about shortening detection, evaluation, and deployment while keeping the process controlled and auditable.
10. System Integration and Future Development Directions These components must be integrated through clear data interfaces, access control, and error handling. Wiring services together does not by itself create an autonomous decision system.
Version 1.0: Observable, Predictable, Maintainable Foundation The first phase gives every component defined inputs and outputs, measurable monitoring, and failure handling, then validates performance on a limited set of devices and lines.
System Phase 1 Focus Evaluation Metrics Real-time streaming platform Establish data acquisition and feature-processing pipelines Throughput, data loss rate, end-to-end latency Anomaly detection Reduce invalid alerts while preserving important events False positive rate, false negative rate, F1 score RUL prediction Estimate equipment health and remaining useful life RMSE, prediction intervals, maintenance decision effectiveness Edge Agent Coordinate models, tools, and maintenance workflows Task success rate, latency, failure recovery capability Industrial RAG Establish document retrieval and answer traceability Retrieval quality, answer correctness, citation traceability MLOps Establish model versioning and release workflows Deployment cycle, rollback time, version traceability completeness Version 2.0: From Single-Equipment Analytics to Cross-Equipment Collaboration Once data processing, model quality, and deployment are stable per device, explore collaboration across devices and lines:
Extend real-time processing to more devices while evaluating bandwidth and compute for higher sampling rates. Combine multiple sensors to improve detection of complex, multi-factor anomalies. Integrate RUL with spare-parts management, maintenance scheduling, and work-order systems. Build an equipment knowledge graph for relationship queries across documents and devices. Let Edge Agents exchange states and task results within their authorized boundaries. Longer term, an Edge Agent Swarm could let multiple agents collaborate across devices or tasks. That adds state consistency, task conflicts, communication failures, access control, and error propagation — so responsibilities, permitted actions, and failure handling must be defined before expanding autonomy.
11. Conclusion Building an Edge-AI system for a smart factory is more than combining sensors, machine-learning models, and an agent framework. The real work is system engineering: reliable data acquisition, models that run within constrained resources, anomaly results worth trusting, safe recovery from failed deployments, and AI recommendations that fit into equipment and maintenance workflows without breaking existing safety mechanisms.
Predictive maintenance and autonomous decision agents are not two separate capabilities. The former provides condition and risk information; the Agent turns it into traceable workflows. Data governance, model monitoring, and safety controls keep the whole system reliable over time.
The priority is not full autonomy from day one. Make each component observable, verifiable, and recoverable first, then expand the scope of AI-assisted decisions — because AI capability and system responsibility boundaries must be defined together for the technology to work on the factory floor.
Appendix: How to Read the Numbers Figures here come from past project experience and interview material. They explain design trade-offs; they are not performance promises.
Source and scope. Some original test records are no longer retrievable, and none of these numbers has been independently revalidated. Company, customer, equipment, and system details are de-identified or generalized. Measurement basis matters more than the number. Latency and cold start depend on start and end points. A false-positive rate depends on whether the denominator is normal samples or all alerts. Availability depends on the window and criteria. Document counts and container image size are equally ambiguous: source documents, versions, or chunks; one service or the full runtime. Read averages with their distribution and tail. Improvement is not attributable to a single cause. Downtime, maintenance cost, abnormal-stop rate, and hours saved are shaped by workflows, spare-parts strategy, equipment upgrades, and staffing. If the model’s contribution cannot be isolated, do not credit all of it to AI. Not industry benchmarks. These figures hold for specific equipment, loads, and deployment conditions. Another line or failure mode can produce entirely different results. Nothing here is a basis for operating specific equipment, implementing safety controls, or making maintenance decisions.
summary:
TL;DR

  • Six-layer architecture: sensing → streaming → signal processing → PHM → Edge Agent → MES/EAP safety integration.
  • Two-stage detection (Isolation Forest → Autoencoder) plus RUL prediction turns raw signals into maintenance planning; figures are project-specific.
  • Models ship through shadow deployment, canary rollout (5% → 20% → 100%), then monitoring and rollback.
  • Edge Agent, Industrial RAG, and MLOps connect evidence to workflows, but safety-critical control stays outside the LLM.

Make each layer observable, verifiable, and recoverable before expanding autonomy.
title: Smart Fab Edge-AI: Predictive Maintenance and Autonomous Decision Agent System
